designs.understanding: The scheme engine is a small pure evaluator (schemes/rules.py, 120 lines) with only two outcomes, so a missing field is folded into 'fails': _apply returns False when the value is None. A second bug sits in the same line: IS_FALSE on a missing value returns True because bool(None) is False, so a missing field passes a negative constraint. The input is two untyped dicts (scheme_schemas.EligibilityIn founder/startup: dict[str, Any]). Their keys are a private convention between seed.py rule paths, the catalogue 'inputs' lists (startup.dpiit vs startup.dpiit_recognized, startup.age_years vs incorporation_age_years) and the Schemes form, and nothing projects conversation slots onto them. Scheme facts live in two copies: seed.py has rules and money fields but no status; the funding catalogue has status and benefit text but no rules. The money fields mix benefit caps, loan sizes and project sizes, and 'grant' is taken to mean non-dilutive. Finally, /talk's support_for never consults the engine: registry._scheme_rules picks schemes from the domain card. The root is one missing contract (typed founder facts with an explicit unknown), one missing join (catalogue status and money meaning onto the rules), and a second, reason-less decision path in the agent.

approaches.name: Kleene three-valued evaluator in the existing rules.py plus a typed FounderFacts contract
approaches.how: Rule evaluation returns Tri (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN); ALL is Kleene AND, ANY is Kleene OR, NONE is NOT(OR). An UNKNOWN leaf records its field path. The engine sorts schemes into eligible / needs_info (with the missing fields) / ineligible (with real violated rules). The input is a Pydantic FounderFacts model whose fields are all Optional.
approaches.basis: Kleene's strong three-valued logic is the standard semantics for unknowns (SQL NULL uses it); the evaluator is ours and 120 lines; Pydantic v2 is already the schema layer.
approaches.advantages: No dependency. The Soundness/Completeness properties are kept and become true. The unknown fields become the next questions. One contract for seed rules, catalogue inputs, slots and forms, and a CI test can check every rule path against the model.
approaches.drawbacks: Every caller and test must handle a third bucket; seed paths and catalogue inputs migrate once.

approaches.name: JsonLogic rules (json-logic-py) over a JSON profile
approaches.how: Re-encode the rule trees as JsonLogic data; evaluate in Python and optionally in the browser.
approaches.basis: JsonLogic is a known portable rule format with ports in many languages.
approaches.advantages: Rules become data; the same rules could run client-side.
approaches.drawbacks: A missing var resolves to null and comparisons go false, so the bug is reproduced, not fixed. The Python port is small and rarely maintained, and every tree must be rewritten.

approaches.name: Answer-set or Datalog engine (clingo / pyDatalog) with open unknown atoms
approaches.how: Encode eligibility as logic rules; unknown facts stay open and the solver reports which atoms would make a scheme derivable.
approaches.basis: Answer-set programming handles incomplete knowledge natively; clingo is mature and pip-installable.
approaches.advantages: Can compute minimal 'what would you need' sets, including across ANY branches.
approaches.drawbacks: A new language and a native dependency for 8 to 46 rules. Reasons are harder to word, and the team must learn ASP. Overkill for a tree evaluator.

approaches.name: Present-only filter or optimistic defaults
approaches.how: Before evaluating, drop schemes with any missing input, or fill missing fields with permissive defaults.
approaches.basis: One-line changes in normalise_profile.
approaches.drawbacks: The filter hides most schemes from an early founder; the defaults invent facts and return false 'yes' answers. Both break 'no invented data' or Soundness.

approaches.name: Catalogue as the single source: rule trees generated from structured catalogue criteria
approaches.how: Give each catalogue entry structured criteria (age bands per category, entity types, stages) and build RuleGroups from them at load, retiring the hand-written seed trees.
approaches.basis: SYSTEM-DESIGN 5.3 already wants schemas for class A data; TASKS 4.1.1 wants one source.
approaches.advantages: One edit point for status, amounts and rules; drift between seed and catalogue becomes impossible.
approaches.drawbacks: Catalogue eligibility is free text today. Structuring 46 entries is curation work that cannot block the logic fix, and generic criteria cannot express every scheme's quirks.

designs.chosen: Kleene three-valued evaluator plus typed FounderFacts (approach 1), with the catalogue joined by id for status, money meaning and the structured criteria of the encoded schemes (a staged step towards approach 5), and support_for routed through the same engine.

design.components: 1) app/core/tri.py (SM1). 2) schemes/rules.py: evaluate(node, facts) -> Verdict. A None value gives UNKNOWN with the field path for every op, including IS_TRUE/IS_FALSE. A TypeError gives UNKNOWN with 'could not compare' logged, never FALSE. 3) app/core/facts.py FounderFacts (SM2). founder fields: state (TNState Literal, normalised for case, whitespace and the 'TN' alias), district (T01 enum), age, date_of_birth, gender, social_category (Literal general/bc/mbc/sc/st/ews/obc; purpose=caste), special_groups (set of ex_servicemen/differently_abled/transgender; purpose=caste), first_graduate, rural, tn_residency_years. startup fields: stage (T01), entity_type, incorporated, incorporation_age_years, dpiit_recognised, startuptn_registered, annual_revenue, sector (T01), women_led. 4) schemes/catalogue.py loads funding_catalogue.json through a Pydantic CatalogueEntry (SM6) and exposes status(id), status_note, checked_on, money(id) and criteria(id). 5) The Scheme dataclass gains project_min, project_max, benefit_max, benefit_rate_pct (optional), dilutive and equity_pct; min_funding/max_funding are removed. 6) engine.check_eligibility returns EligibilityResult(eligible, needs_info[(scheme, missing_fields)], ineligible, not_open[(scheme, status, status_note)]). 7) agents/tools.py _support_for(session, domain_id, district): registry routes become a relevance shortlist ('why relevant'), and the engine decides eligibility on FounderFacts.from_slots(session).redact(consents).
design.data_model: FounderFacts (Pydantic, extra='forbid', all Optional). Verdict{value: Tri, failed: list[str], unknown: list[str]}. For encoded schemes the catalogue entry adds 'criteria' {age: {general: [21,45], special: [21,55], special_groups: [...]}, stages: [...], entity_types: [...]}, plus 'project_min', 'project_max', 'benefit_max', 'benefit_rate_pct', 'dilutive' and 'equity_pct'; 'inputs' is rewritten to FounderFacts paths. SchemeOut adds status, status_note, checked_on, dilutive, equity_pct, benefit_max and the project range. RecommendOut adds needs_info[{scheme, missing:[{field, question}]}] and not_open[].
design.algorithm: Kleene logic: AND = FALSE if any child is FALSE, else UNKNOWN if any is UNKNOWN, else TRUE. OR = TRUE if any child is TRUE, else UNKNOWN if any is UNKNOWN, else FALSE. NONE = NOT(OR). A FALSE result carries only the violated labels of its FALSE children; an UNKNOWN result carries the field paths of the UNKNOWN children that could still change the outcome. Bucketing order: status outside {active, cohort, between_calls, announced} -> not_open with the catalogue note (closed, revamping, not_in_tn, lapsed_pending, unverified); otherwise TRUE -> eligible, UNKNOWN -> needs_info, FALSE -> ineligible. Eligible schemes with status between_calls or cohort are labelled 'next call expected' or 'check the current call'. Funding fit compares funding_need with [project_min, project_max]. The 'why' line states 'about Rs X of your Rs Y' (min(rate*need, cap)) only when benefit_rate_pct and benefit_max are curated; otherwise it shows the cap. 'non-dilutive' is said only for type GRANT with dilutive False; TANSEED says 'equity-linked grant (3% stake)'. NEEDS/UYEGP ages become ANY(ALL(category general, age in general band), ALL(category or special group in the special list, age in special band)). With an unknown category and age 40, NEEDS gives UNKNOWN (needs category) instead of a wrong yes or no.
design.interfaces: Depends on T01 (Stage, Sector, District enums and mappings) and T03 (typed slot values with source rank, for from_slots). Provides SM1 to T29/T09/T24 and SM2 to T29/T24/T19. T19's purpose gate calls FounderFacts.redact before evaluation. T24's card pre-check calls check_eligibility per card. annotate.py and the planner milestone annotation (1.4.1.1) consume the eligible list and status labels.
design.rollout: 1) tri.py and the evaluator, keeping the existing dict input behind the same API (the response gains needs_info). 2) FounderFacts, with a compatibility constructor from the old dict keys for one release that logs a warning on legacy keys. 3) The catalogue join and money fields. 4) support_for. designs.understanding: Two separate problems share one cause: the supply side is not anchored in the one real data source (the MCA directory) and its limits. (a) /b2b/decompose builds the supply map with match_demand over SEED_SUPPLY (invented suppliers), so 'matched' and 'gap' are defined against invented companies while the real nearby_makers sit unused in the same response. The cluster hint is an uncited constant in Supply.tsx. The directory covers only Chennai, Coimbatore and Madurai but does not say so, and when the founder's PIN is unknown it falls back to name order. (b) The CP-SAT allocation objective mixes scales. SHORT_PENALTY of 10,000,000 paise is only Rs 1 lakh, so expensive items go unbought with a false reason. FAR_PENALTY and TRUST_BONUS are flat rupees whatever the price. A minimum order above the need is a dead end, and inputs are not validated (duplicate ids, category case). All member flags hold on the current code.

approaches.name: Directory-only supply map with a three-valued gap and cited reference files

Cluster pointers and district centroids are Git-held, cited JSON files in the backend; the frontend renders what the API returns.

approaches.name: Lexicographic CP-SAT (two or three solves)
approaches.how: Solve 1 maximises placed units, and that optimum is fixed as a constraint. Solve 2 minimises landed cost (price plus founder-entered delivery), and that optimum is fixed too. Solve 3 maximises local and trusted choices as a tie-breaker among cost-optimal plans.
approaches.basis: The standard lexicographic (pre-emptive) multi-objective method; OR-Tools CP-SAT is already in the stack; the models are tiny (20 lines x 100 quotes).
approaches.advantages: Correct for any price scale with no magic constants; every preference is explainable, in order.
approaches.drawbacks: Two to three solves (milliseconds each at this size).

approaches.name: Single weighted objective with a data-derived big-M and percentage penalties
approaches.how: Penalty per short unit = (max unit price + max penalties) * 100 + 1; distance and trust as a percentage of the unit price.
approaches.basis: Common big-M practice in MIP modelling.
approaches.drawbacks: Large coefficients at 10^7 units risk overflow or slow search; the percentages are invented tuning numbers presented as 'rules'.

approaches.name: Keep seed matching with an 'example' label; add quote-fed scoring later
approaches.how: Label invented suppliers as examples; when the founder's quotes move server-side (3.1.3), score them with the 40/30/20/10 scorer.
approaches.basis: Minimal change.
approaches.drawbacks: Invented companies and prices stay in front of founders, the gap stays meaningless, and the owner's D9 preference is 'not fetched' over labelled demos.

approaches.name: PostGIS spatial index over the full MCA file
approaches.how: Load all 78,689 companies into PostgreSQL with geometry and query by distance.
approaches.basis: PostGIS is the standard spatial extension.
approaches.advantages: Scales and ranks by true distance.
approaches.drawbacks: Reference data lives in Git by design, the database is not live yet (2.1.1), and haversine over a few thousand rows in Python is already fast enough.

approaches.basis: Commercial APIs.
approaches.drawbacks: Violates the free/offline constraint; India Post PIN centroids give enough precision for 'nearest' at district scale.

design.algorithm: Gap: if the founder's district is not in the directory's districts -> outside_coverage (UNKNOWN) with 'our directory covers Chennai, Coimbatore and Madurai today'. Else if the directory has 0 makers for the category -> gap (FALSE), and the cluster hint fires (4.2.2). Else covered (TRUE). No reach threshold is invented: makers are listed with km and the founder judges. Allocation: stage 1 maximises sum(x) and adds sum(x) == best. Stage 2 minimises sum((price + delivery) * 100 * x) in paise and adds cost == best2. Stage 3 maximises sum(local[s] * x) + sum(trusted[s] * y) as a tie-breaker. why_unmet comes from the stage-1 model: capacity, MOQ, budget, or 'no supplier with known prices'. 'Capacity taken by your other lines' is said only when another line actually uses that supplier. MOQ alternative: for each unmet line and each same-category supplier whose min_order is above the need and whose remaining capacity after the solve is at least min_order, offer 'buy min_order: extra units, extra cost', cheapest first.

designs.understanding: Auth works for a demo but has no production guard. secret_key defaults to 'change-me' and nothing refuses it (is_production exists but is unused), so tokens can be forged in any deployment that forgets the variable. Refresh tokens carry a jti that nothing stores; the frontend never calls /auth/refresh; there is no logout; and refresh does not invalidate the old token. Login skips bcrypt for unknown emails and register answers 409, so accounts can be enumerated. The rate limiter keys by request.state.user_id, which nothing sets, so everything is keyed by the raw client IP: shared under carrier NAT and behind any proxy. The per-key dict is never pruned, limits are per worker process, and every request (a cheap GET, SSE notices, a TTS sentence) costs the same; a 429 on the notices EventSource kills it for good. The single root: the server has no notion of who is calling (a principal) and keeps no durable server-side token state.

flags_disputed.note: The login half holds and is a two-line fix. The register half cannot be fully closed without email verification, which is not available offline or free: with any 'generic' register reply, a prober can register and then log in to learn whether the email already existed. Resolved by constant-time login, a generic register message, strict per-email-hash and per-IP auth budgets, and a documented residual risk until email delivery exists.

Holds. The recommendation's reason for ruling out Redis is right: Redis is optional here, so revocation must be durable in PostgreSQL. Sign-in already needs the users table, so this adds no new availability dependency.

approaches.name: Principal middleware plus Redis-or-memory window counters with route cost classes (in-house)
approaches.how: One middleware resolves the principal: the verified bearer sub (no DB hit), else the session id in agent/voice paths, else the client IP, honouring only trusted proxies. Limits are per class (turn, speak, notices-connect, auth, default) and per principal, counted in Redis INCR+EXPIRE fixed windows with a bounded in-process dict as fallback. An IP backstop cap applies to session and anonymous principals.
approaches.basis: The same INCR+EXPIRE pattern as research/sources.py _over_budget; Redis rate limits are in SYSTEM-DESIGN 4.1 L1; the Starlette middleware is already in place.
approaches.advantages: Fair under CGNAT, shared across workers, memory bounded by TTL, no new dependency, and testable through the in-memory fallback without a Redis server.
approaches.drawbacks: Fixed windows allow a burst at a window edge (acceptable at these limits), and we own a little code.

approaches.name: slowapi / limits library
approaches.how: Decorate routes with per-route limits, with Redis or memory storage and a key function that returns the principal.
approaches.basis: A popular port of Flask-Limiter for Starlette/FastAPI; limits supports moving windows.
approaches.advantages: Moving windows and per-route rules are prebuilt.
approaches.drawbacks: A new dependency and decorator changes across routers; the keying decision (the principal) still has to be written; its key format differs from SYSTEM-DESIGN's Redis key table.

approaches.name: Reverse-proxy limiting (nginx limit_req / Caddy rate_limit)
approaches.how: Limit at the proxy by IP or header.
approaches.basis: The standard production pattern.
approaches.drawbacks: Hosting is undecided; the proxy cannot see the JWT subject or session cheaply; not testable in the repo or in local runs.

approaches.name: DB-backed rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection, plus a single-flight refresh in the client
approaches.how: A refresh_tokens table (hashed jti, family_id, user_id, expires_at, revoked_at, replaced_by). /refresh rotates and revokes the presented token; presenting a revoked token revokes its whole family; /logout revokes. api.ts retries once on 401 after one shared refresh call.
approaches.basis: Refresh-token rotation with reuse detection from the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP; SQLAlchemy/Alembic are already used.
approaches.advantages: Durable revocation without Redis; logout works server-side; theft is detected; fits erasure (delete by user).
approaches.drawbacks: One DB write per refresh (every 30 minutes per active user: negligible).

approaches.name: fastapi-users or an external identity provider
approaches.how: Adopt a full auth package or a hosted IdP for tokens, refresh, reset and verification.
approaches.basis: fastapi-users is popular; hosted IdPs (Auth0, Clerk) are mature.
approaches.cost: free/open source (fastapi-users); paid beyond free tiers and online (hosted IdPs)
approaches.drawbacks: Replaces the working User model and services (a large migration); hosted IdPs break free/offline and send founder identities to a third party.

approaches.name: Asymmetric signing (EdDSA/RS256) with a key ring
approaches.how: Sign with a private key and verify with public keys selected by kid.
approaches.basis: python-jose supports it.
approaches.advantages: Verification keys can be shared; rotation by kid.
approaches.drawbacks: No second verifier service exists, so it is key-management overhead for no gain now.

designs.chosen: Approach 1 (principal middleware and in-house window counters with cost classes) combined with approach 4 (durable rotating refresh tokens and a single-flight client refresh), plus a production settings guard with a two-key verification window for rotation, and constant-time login.
designs.why_chosen: Both halves fix the root: the server finally knows who is calling (the principal, SM5) and keeps token state durably. The principal is also what T19 needs for the consent subject and T17 for owner checks, so one middleware serves three themes. The window counters reuse the research-budget Redis pattern and degrade to bounded memory when Redis is off, matching the optional-Redis stack. PostgreSQL refresh state adds no availability dependency, because sign-in already needs the users table. A previous-key verification window (SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS) makes rotation possible without logging everyone out: the cheap part of a key ring, without asymmetric keys.

not_chosen.name: Asymmetric keys with a full key ring
not_chosen.reason: No second verifier exists; the two-key HS256 window gives rotation for a fraction of the work.

design.components: 1) core/config.py: a model_validator(mode='after') that refuses a secret_key in a denylist ('change-me', '', 'secret') or shorter than 32 bytes when app_env != 'development'. An optional secret_key_previous. In production the same guard reports the other dev defaults (postgres password, MinIO keys) as errors. 2) core/security.py: decode_token tries secret_key, then secret_key_previous; tokens carry a kid fingerprint for logging. 3) models/refresh_token.py + migration: refresh_tokens(id, user_id FK, jti_hash sha256, family_id, issued_at, expires_at, revoked_at, replaced_by). 4) services/auth_service.py: issuing stores the refresh jti; refresh rotates (revokes the old token and issues a new one in the same family); reuse of a revoked jti revokes the family and returns 401 TOKEN_REUSED; logout revokes the family. authenticate_user verifies against a module-level dummy bcrypt hash when the user is missing. On a duplicate, register returns the same 202 and message as a fresh registration ('If this email is new, the account is ready; sign in'). 5) routers/auth.py: POST /logout. 6) core/identity.py IdentityMiddleware (SM5) sets the principal: the bearer token, decoded without a DB hit (an invalid token means anonymous, and the route still rejects it); else the session id parsed from /api/v1/ideation/agent/sessions/{id}/...; else the IP. Trusted proxies come from settings.forwarded_allow_ips via uvicorn's ProxyHeadersMiddleware. 7) core/counters.py: hit(key, window_s, limit) -> (allowed, remaining, reset), using a Redis INCR+EXPIRE pipeline, else an in-process dict pruned on access and capped (oldest windows evicted). 8) core/middleware.py: RateLimitMiddleware rewritten around route classes. 9) Frontend: api.ts does a single-flight refresh on 401, then one retry; auth.tsx logs out via /logout; agentClient.ts listenNotices reconnects with backoff on error and resumes notices.
design.data_model: Principal{kind: user|session|ip, id, ip}. Route classes in settings: turn (stream POST: 30/min per principal); speak (voice/speak: 120/min per session); notices (EventSource connect: 10/min per session; the open stream is not counted again); auth (login/register/refresh: 10/min per IP and 5/min per email hash); default (100/min per principal). ip_backstop: 600/min for session and anonymous principals. The per-worker global guard is kept. Redis keys rl:{class}:{kind}:{id}:{window_start} with TTL = window. refresh_tokens as above.
design.algorithm: Per request: classify the route, resolve the principal, then call counters.hit for the principal's limit and, for session/ip principals, the IP backstop. A refusal returns 429 with Retry-After = seconds to the window reset, and logs a structured rate_limited{class, kind} event so 5.4.1 sees rejected turns. Refresh rotation: look up jti_hash; missing or expired -> 401; revoked -> revoke the family and return 401 TOKEN_REUSED; otherwise revoke it and issue a new pair in the same family, in one transaction. Client: concurrent 401s share one in-flight refresh promise; if the refresh fails, the tokens are cleared.
design.interfaces: The SM5 principal is used by T19 (consent subject: user or session) and T17 (owner checks on session routes). counters.hit is reused by the research source budgets (theme of F-B5-001). Erasure (3.2.4) deletes refresh_tokens by user. Claiming a session (3.1.1) changes the principal from session to user; the keys are separate, so limits are not reset unfairly.
design.rollout: 1) The settings guard and constant-time login (no DB needed; TASKS 3.1.4). 2) The principal middleware and counters, with limits read from settings so they can be tuned without code. 3) The refresh table, rotation, logout and the client wrapper together, once the users table is live (3.1.1/2.1.1). The runbook is updated in the same PR as SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS.
design.offline: No network calls. Redis is optional (bounded memory fallback; the health endpoint notes that limits are then per worker). PostgreSQL is needed only for sign-in, which already needs it.

designs.understanding: Experience mode (EntryMode.EXPERIENCE) is idea mode with three slots dropped and four promoted. Its REQUIRED set has 10 slots against Q_MAX = 7, so district, assets and motivation are never asked. The questions are worded for an idea ('Which sector does this sit in?'), and money is asked before skills, against the plan's rule that financial questions wait on consent. The state machine goes CONFIRMING -> GENERATING with the self-description as the idea, so there is no step where the founder sees and chooses an opportunity. Research runs on 'I worked 12 years as a cook in Salem' once it passes 20 characters. On the data side, registry cards have no field that experience can match (skills, assets) and no citations, and 190 of 240 cards are drafts. The root: the mode was modelled as a different required set rather than as a different flow (describe yourself -> ranked, cited cards -> choose -> idea flow).

An invariant test checks len(REQUIRED_BY_MODE[m]) <= Q_MAX for every mode, and an ordering test checks that no financial slot precedes founder_skills. 2) elicitation/session.py: SessionState.CHOOSING; ElicitationSession.choice: Choice{kind: 'card'|'lever', options: [ids], shown_at, chosen: id|None, round: int}. 3) elicitation/engine.py: confirming in EXPERIENCE goes to CHOOSING with ranked cards. choose(card_id) writes problem/solution/sector/product_form/beneficiary from the card with Source.CARD (ranked below ANSWER in T03); the mode stays EXPERIENCE, but the required set switches to the idea set minus what is filled, then ELICITING or CONFIRMING. 'None fit' gives the next round of cards excluding those shown (at most 2 rounds), then offers switching to idea mode while keeping all confirmed slots. 4) planner/opportunity.py (new): rank(facts) over cards with review in {base, approved} and non-empty sources. 5) Registry data: cards gain skills_used (tags), assets_used (tags) and sources [{url, title, checked_on}]; categories.json gains a skills vocabulary {tag: {label, synonyms_en, synonyms_ta}} and an assets vocabulary; elicitation/extract.py maps founder_skills/owned_assets free text to tags by whole-word synonym match (T01 cue rules). 6) agents/ideation.py: the research trigger requires mode IDEA or choice.chosen; choose sets s.idea = card label + summary and clears s.scan so 1.2.3 versioning runs a fresh scan; the snapshot exposes the pending choice. 7) routers/ideation.py: AgentStartIn.mode (EntryMode) and a choose action shared with 1.2.4 (POST .../choice {option_id | 'none'}); Start.tsx routes founders with no idea to experience mode.
design.data_model: Choice as above, in the elicitation document (a T34 format step adds choice: null). Card fields: skills_used: list[str], assets_used: list[str], sources: list[Source], review. Ranked card: {domain_id, label, summary, score, terms: {skills: matched tags, assets: matched tags, district: fit or 'not rated for your district', capital: within|above|unknown}, schemes: T04 buckets, sources}.
design.algorithm: Score = 0.4 * skill_overlap + 0.2 * asset_overlap + 0.25 * district_fit + 0.15 * capital_fit, each in [0,1]. skill_overlap = |founder_tags & skills_used| / |skills_used|; asset_overlap likewise, and when the card needs no assets the term is dropped and the weights renormalised. district_fit = card.districts[d][0] / 3, or UNKNOWN when the card has no rating for that district (term dropped, shown as 'not rated for your district', never as 1). capital_fit = 1 if the card's capital_band <= the founder's, 0 if above, UNKNOWN when capital was not asked (no financial consent). The weights are documented as the ranking policy and shown in each card's 'why'. Ties are broken by the number of cited sources, then id. The top 3 are spoken (5 on screen); a card with zero skill overlap is never shown. Scheme pre-check: check_eligibility(FounderFacts.from_slots(session).redact(consents)) restricted to the card's registry routes, three-valued.
design.interfaces: Depends on T05 (the question policy honours the required set, purposes and per-mode text), T01 (sector and district vocabularies, whole-word cue matching), T03 (Source.CARD rank), T04 (engine pre-check), T19 (purpose tags) and T34 (format step for choice and CHOOSING). designs.understanding: The Funding screen hard-codes 'richer defaults' (has_ip, retention 60, runway 12, unit economics, a cap table and more) that supply most of the points in four of the six readiness dimensions. readiness.py treats a missing input as zero, so without the defaults scores are falsely low and with them falsely high. The overall score then gates investors through an invented threshold (60 for every stage that is not late), so idea and prototype founders see no investor. Investors whose stages or sectors are unpublished are rejected as 'no', and 60% of the fit score is constants (stage always 100, geography always 100, track always 60). The gap plan adds whole playbooks without checking what the founder already has, with impact points that disagree with the rubric. Pipeline metrics count a lost deal as reaching every stage, and lose the first stage's time because date.fromisoformat cannot parse the browser's ISO timestamps. One root: unknown is treated as a value (zero, yes or no) instead of being carried as unknown, and numbers are asserted instead of derived from the rubric or the data.

approaches.name: Unknown-aware scoring: interval readiness, three-valued investor constraints, counterfactual gaps
approaches.how: Readiness terms declare their input and maximum points. An unknown input contributes [0, max], so each dimension and the overall score are intervals, and a band is stated only when both ends fall in it. Investor constraints are Tri: published and violated = no; unpublished = 'check with the investor'. Readiness becomes advice, not a gate, and fit uses only terms that vary. Gap impact = score(after the action) - score(before), using the same function, so actions whose input is already at its target drop out.
approaches.basis: Interval arithmetic is the numeric form of Kleene logic (SM1); the rubric is a pure function, so counterfactual re-scoring is exact and cheap.
approaches.advantages: Honest numbers with no invented inputs; the interval width shows what to answer next; gap points agree with the score by construction; idea-stage founders see pre-seed investors.
approaches.drawbacks: Founders see ranges instead of a single number; each playbook action needs an input mapping.

designs.why_chosen: It removes invented inputs and thresholds at the root, using the same unknown-aware machinery as schemes (SM1: Tri for constraints, Interval for scores) and the same FounderFacts contract (SM2), so the conversation's stage, team and traction answers fill readiness without asking again. Counterfactual impacts make gap advice and the score agree by construction, and actions already done disappear automatically, so one mechanism fixes both gap flaws. The pipeline fixes are standard-library changes.

design.components: 1) funding/readiness.py: the rubric as data, TERMS[dimension] = [Term(input, kind: bool|num, points(value), max_points)]. score_readiness(inputs) -> ReadinessResult{dimensions: {name: {lo, hi, known: [...], missing: [...], assessed: bool}}, overall: Interval, band: str|None, band_range: (band_lo, band_hi)}. A dimension with no known input is 'not assessed'. 2) The input is FundingFacts (part of SM2 FounderFacts: stage, team_size, founder_experience_years, users, monthly_revenue, is_registered, dpiit_recognised, has_pitch_deck, ...), all Optional; from_slots fills stage, team and traction from the session. 3) funding/gaps.py: playbook rows declare the inputs they set {input: value} and an effort label. For each row whose target differs from the current known value (or the value is unknown), impact = overall.lo(after) - overall.lo(before). Rows with impact 0 are dropped; the rest are ordered by impact, with effort shown as a 'rough guide'. 4) funding/investor_match.py: constraints return Tri via core/tri.py, grouped as eligible / check_with_investor ('stage not published: ask them') / ineligible. readiness_gate is deleted and replaced by an advice line from gaps. Fit is a weighted mean over varying terms only: sector (specialist 1.0, generalist 0.8); stage position (1.0 if the founder's stage is the earliest in the investor's list, otherwise 0.7); traction margin above the floor; ticket position within the range. Geography and track record are omitted until the data varies; weights are renormalised over known terms, and the terms are listed. 5) funding/pipeline.py: _parse(at) = datetime.fromisoformat(at).date() (Python 3.11 accepts 'Z'), and date-only strings are also accepted. _reached for a terminal entry without history = {initial_contact, terminal}. weighted_value and STAGE_PROBABILITY are removed and value_by_stage added. 6) Funding.tsx sends only the fields the founder set ('not sure' sends null), and shows ranges, 'not assessed' dimensions, the next inputs to answer, and the investor list in three groups.
design.data_model: Interval{lo:int, hi:int}. ReadinessOut: dimensions[{name, lo, hi, assessed, missing}], overall{lo, hi}, band|null, band_range. Recommendation{dimension, action, sets, impact_points, effort_label}. InvestorMatchOut: eligible[{investor, fit, terms}], check_with_investor[{investor, unknown}], ineligible[{investor, reasons}]. PipelineMetrics: weighted_value removed, value_by_stage added.
design.algorithm: Readiness: a known term adds points(value) to both lo and hi; an unknown term adds 0 to lo and max_points to hi. Each dimension is clamped to 0..100, and overall = the weighted sum of the lo values and of the hi values. A band is shown when band(lo) == band(hi). The next input to ask is the missing input with the largest weight * max_points (the interval width it removes), which feeds T05's value of asking. Investors: Kleene AND over the constraints; an unknown ticket is already UNKNOWN; not_investing is FALSE. Gaps: counterfactual re-score on the lower bound, so an action on an unknown input is phrased 'if you have not done this yet' and its impact is the points it would add.
design.interfaces: Depends on T01 (stage and sector vocabularies; readiness _STAGE_SCORE and investor stages map through the canonical Stage). Uses SM1 and SM2. T19's redact applies to the financial inputs (monthly_revenue, runway) under the financial purpose. The pipeline board moving server-side (3.1.3) and the programme aggregates (5.5.5) inherit the corrected metrics.
design.rollout: 1) Pipeline fixes (independent and small). 2) Remove the Funding.tsx defaults together with interval readiness, in one PR (removing the defaults alone would make scores falsely low). 3) Three-valued investor groups and removal of the gate. 4) Counterfactual gaps. API fields change shape, so the frontend is updated in the same PRs.
design.offline: All deterministic and local; investor data is Git-held; no model is involved beyond wording.

designs.understanding: AgentSession.to_dict/from_dict read and write a fixed key list with no format number. Stores call from_dict directly, so any undecodable document raises (ValidationError, KeyError) into a 500, and /cohort/programme loads up to 500 documents in one comprehension, so one bad document fails the whole aggregate. Older code silently drops keys it does not know when it loads and saves (rollbacks, workers on mixed versions, the 6-hour Redis copy). Unknown enum strings are kept as bare str under contextlib.suppress, so renamed sectors (D5, 4.1.2) survive as dead values that also feed idea_version, which keys background results. Upgrade-on-read (2.1.4 as planned) never rewrites rows nobody opens, and there is no format column, so the planned table split (5.5.5) would face every historical format, with no rule for staying in step with the live JSON. Root: no format contract (a version number, one decode, a pure upgrade chain, a newer-format guard, a queryable column, and a backfill).

flags_disputed.note: Holds. Also, SqlStore.get merges row.version into the document; decode must treat the row columns (version, format) as authoritative over the copies inside the document.

approaches.name: Format number, one decode, a pure upgrade chain, a newer-format guard, a format column and an upgrade-all script
approaches.how: A FORMAT constant; documents carry 'format'. decode(raw) upgrades step by step with pure functions and raises UndecodableSession or NewerFormat, which stores and routers map to 410/skip and 503. Saves refuse when the stored format is newer. A format column records the format, and an idempotent script rewrites old rows. The table split is a derived projection from upgraded JSON.
approaches.basis: Schema-version reader rules (Avro/Protobuf compatibility, Django and Rails data migrations), expand/contract with backfill (SYSTEM-DESIGN 5.2), and a CQRS read model for the split.
approaches.advantages: Small, in one module, testable on the memory store; visible failures instead of silent loss; the split sees one format.
approaches.drawbacks: During a rollback, newer sessions are unavailable until the roll-forward; one more migration and one script.

approaches.name: The whole session as a Pydantic model with lenient validators and extra='allow'
approaches.how: Replace the dataclass with a Pydantic model whose defaults and coercions absorb old shapes, keeping extra keys.
approaches.basis: Pydantic v2 already models the elicitation part.
approaches.advantages: A declarative shape; unknown keys preserved.
approaches.drawbacks: A large refactor; leniency hides real corruption; old code still acts wrongly on fields it ignores (retention ignoring 'saved').

approaches.name: Preserve unknown keys only (an extras dict round-tripped)
approaches.how: from_dict stores unrecognised keys and to_dict writes them back.
approaches.basis: Protobuf's unknown-field preservation.
approaches.drawbacks: Old code still makes decisions blind to new fields (consent, saved), which is worse than refusing.

approaches.name: Alembic data migrations with frozen upgrader copies, or jsonb_set SQL
approaches.how: Each format change is an Alembic migration that rewrites the JSONB in SQL or with a frozen copy of the Python upgrader.
approaches.basis: Common Alembic practice; native PostgreSQL JSONB functions.
approaches.drawbacks: Duplicated upgrade logic; large JSONB rewrites inside a migration transaction; nested enum mapping is awkward in SQL; untestable on the memory store.

approaches.name: Dual-write normalised tables in SqlStore.save, or PostgreSQL triggers/generated columns
approaches.how: Write the split tables in the same transaction, or derive them in the database.
approaches.basis: SQLAlchemy unit of work; native PostgreSQL features.
approaches.drawbacks: A heavier live path with more failure modes (the rewrite SYSTEM-DESIGN rules out). Triggers hide logic in SQL and cannot run on the memory store, and nested arrays do not suit generated columns.

designs.chosen: Approach 1: a format number with one decode and a pure upgrade chain; a newer-format guard on load and save; a format column with an idempotent upgrade-all script; enum mapping steps that also re-key idea_version results; and the table split as a nightly derived projection from upgraded JSON (decision record).
designs.why_chosen: It addresses every symptom at the root with the least machinery: one module owns the format, every store goes through it, failures are visible and contained, and the backfill gives the split a single format. It is the shared mechanism (SM4) other themes need: T19 adds consent events and T24 adds the CHOOSING choice as registered steps, and T01's sector mapping becomes a step instead of an ad-hoc rewrite. The projection keeps decision 0003 (one document, one write per turn) intact.

design.components: 1) agents/session_format.py (new; no app imports beyond pure helpers): FORMAT = 2 initially, and documents without 'format' are format 1. UPGRADES: dict[int, Callable[[dict], dict]], each step pure and idempotent. decode(raw: dict, *, row_version=None) -> Decoded{session, upgraded_from, idea_version_before}; errors UndecodableSession(session_id, format, reason) and NewerFormat(session_id, format). 2) AgentSession.to_dict writes 'format': FORMAT; from_dict only builds the dataclass from an already-upgraded dict. Enum restore is strict: an unknown value left after upgrading logs session.unknown_enum, and the slot is kept with a confidence below the filled floor so it is asked again (never left as a bare str). 3) All three stores (Memory, Sql, Cached) call decode; CachedStore treats a Redis copy that fails to decode, or is older than the row, as a miss and drops it. 4) Save guard: SqlStore.save adds WHERE format <= FORMAT and writes format=FORMAT; MemoryStore compares the stored document's format; a refusal raises NewerFormat (503 'this conversation was saved by a newer version; try again shortly'). 5) Routers: _load maps UndecodableSession to 410 'cannot be resumed' with a log event; cohort.programme uses store.get_many / decode per row, and skips and counts sessions_unreadable. 6) Migration 0005_session_format adds agent_sessions.format as a nullable, indexed int; the script backfills it; a later migration sets NOT NULL default 1. 7) scripts/upgrade_sessions.py processes batches of N rows WHERE format < FORMAT: decode, then save with the version check (retrying on conflict), with --dry-run and a report of counts per source format and failures. 8) Enum-mapping steps carry a frozen mapping table from T01 (old -> new) as data. The same step switches idea_version to hashing canonical codes; decode reports idea_version_before/after, and the store calls results.rekey(session_id, old, new) once. 9) Decision record 0011: the split tables are a derived projection, rebuilt nightly from documents at format >= N, with Pydantic contracts for the novelty/council/roadmap payloads validated in the projection (a bad payload is skipped and counted).
design.data_model: The document gains 'format': int. Column agent_sessions.format int (indexed). ResultStore gains rekey(session_id, old_iv, new_iv). Projection tables (5.5.5) are derived and can be dropped.
design.algorithm: decode: f = raw.get('format', 1); if f > FORMAT -> NewerFormat; while f < FORMAT: raw = UPGRADES[f](copy(raw)), f += 1; then raw['format'] = f. Building AgentSession, any ValidationError, KeyError, ValueError or TypeError becomes UndecodableSession, logged with the session id, format and exception type, never the document text. Save: refuse if the stored format > FORMAT; write FORMAT. Backfill: idempotent, because decoding a current document is the identity and saves are version-checked.
design.interfaces: Depends on T07 (store contract: get/get_many/save semantics, outage behaviour) and T01 (sector/stage mapping tables). Provides the step registry used by T19 (the consents field from cohort_consent) and T24 (the choice field and CHOOSING state), and decode for T17's owner checks and the 3.2.5.5 get_many. Logging follows 2.4.2 (ids only).
design.rollout: 1) Ship decode with FORMAT=2 (step 1->2 only adds the key) and the guard, with every store using it. 2) The migration adding the nullable format column, then the script, then the constraint. 3) Each later format change lands as a step, a fixture and a test in one PR. Deploys only roll forward; during a rollback window newer sessions return 503 instead of losing data. 4) Before 5.5.5, run the script until COUNT(format < FORMAT) = 0, then build the projection.
design.offline: Pure Python; runs on the memory store and in tests. The script needs only the database it upgrades.

designs.tests: Fixture documents for every historical format decode to the same AgentSession as a fresh session with those facts. decode is idempotent on current documents. Corrupt fixtures raise UndecodableSession and never a 500. NewerFormat on load and save across the Memory, Sql (SQLite JSON variant) and Cached stores. Script dry run and idempotency. rekey keeps results. A projection rebuild equals a from-scratch rebuild.
designs.risks: A buggy upgrade step could corrupt many documents at once during the backfill: the script runs dry first, writes are version-checked, and steps are tested against fixtures before release. During a rollback window, sessions touched by the newer release return 503: documented in the deploy runbook, with format bumps kept rare and additive. Asking again for unmapped enum values annoys returning founders, but it only happens when T01's mapping misses a value, which the mapping test should prevent.
